name: Axillary sweat gland suction

lead: Sweat gland suction aims at permanently drier underarms and less odor by physically removing the glands that produce sweat.

Through small incisions, glands are removed or disrupted by suction or curettage, so they can no longer produce sweat. Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article lists suction, curettage, liposuction-type removal and laser ablation among surgical options, and related procedures are used for underarm odor. The available record includes two small registered trials.

paras: A surgeon performs it as a minor procedure for heavy underarm sweating or odor, typically considered after topical and injection options. Recovery follows the usual course for small surgical incisions.
General surgical risks apply, including pain, bleeding and infection. Specific complication data were not available in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: This minor surgery removes or disrupts underarm sweat glands through small incisions, aiming at lasting dryness and less odor. Data come from small registered trials.

lead: Axillary sweat gland suction, also called suction-curettage or liposuction-type removal, is a minor surgical approach to underarm sweating in which sweat glands in the armpit are physically removed or disrupted through small incisions [1].

Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article lists axillary sweat gland removal or destruction by suction, curettage, liposuction-type removal or laser ablation among surgical options [1]. Related procedures are also used for underarm odor (osmidrosis) [2].
The available record contains two small registered trials and no published results summaries, so evidence for this entry in this wiki is limited to what those registrations describe.

paras: Surgical approaches remove or destroy the glands rather than blocking their nerve signal. Reference sources group suction, curettage and laser ablation together as axillary gland procedures [1].

A registered trial (NCT01274611, 20 participants, started 2010) studied botulinum toxin and suction-curettage for axillary hyperhidrosis [3]. Another registration (NCT01539460, 30 participants, started 2012, status unknown) examined combined liposuction with subcutaneous pruning for axillary osmidrosis [2]. Results are not described in the available record.
Specific adverse-event data for this procedure are not available in the reviewed material.
